text: Both of Girodet's parents died when he was a young adult. His guardian, the physician Benoît-François Trioson, took charge of his education and later adopted him, and in 1812 Girodet took the surname Trioson. He first studied architecture and pursued a military career before turning to painting under a teacher named Luquin. He then entered the school of Jacques-Louis David. At 22 he competed successfully with a painting of the Story of Joseph and his Brethren. From 1789 to 1793 he lived in Italy, and in Rome he painted Endymion, now in the Louvre.

Crome, known as Old Crome to tell him apart from his artist son, lived in Norwich all his life. The son of a weaver, he worked from the age of 12 as an errand boy for a doctor before being apprenticed to Francis Whisler, a painter of houses and coaches. A friendship with the apprentice printer Robert Ladbrooke followed. The two shared a room and went on sketching trips around Norwich. Most of his works are Norfolk landscapes, and he also produced etchings and taught art.

Graff, the seventh child of a craftsman, grew up in Winterthur. In 1753 he began to study painting at the art school of Johann Ulrich Schellenberg, and after three years he left for Augsburg to work with the etcher Johann Jakob Haid. He was too successful there. The painters guild feared his competition, so he had to leave within a year. With a letter from Haid he moved to Ansbach and worked for the court painter Leonhard Schneider until 1759. His portrait subjects included Friedrich Schiller and Gotthold Ephraim Lessing.

Bürkel grew up in Pirmasens, where his father kept an inn that gave him subjects in great variety. In his eleventh year he came into conflict with the police over a caricature of Napoleon. He was meant for trade and at fifteen entered the law, but at twenty he turned to art and learned oil painting among friends in Munich and the Netherlands. In time he depicted popular and military scenes, cattle and landscapes. He lived in Rome from 1823 to 1832. In 2010 three of his paintings were returned to the Pirmasens Museum.

According to Arnold Houbraken, Verkolje became a self-taught artist after hurting himself with darts as a child. The injury to his heel did not heal well. He was bedridden for years, and to pass the time he copied prints, some of them given to him by Jan Gerritsz van Bronckhorst. He later studied for about half a year with Jan Andrea Lievens. The son of an Amsterdam locksmith, he spent his working life in Delft, where he had access to powerful patrons. He is mainly known for portraits and genre pieces of elegant couples in interiors.

Engelbrecht trained as a copper engraver under Gabriel Eigner in Augsburg. He began working alongside his older brother Christian, an established engraver. In his early years he produced portraits of monarchs and detailed landscapes. A period in Vienna proved influential. There he worked on imperial ceremonies and refined his technique, and beginning in 1730 he produced perspective theaters, also called paper theaters or dioramas, which were hand-colored engravings arranged in layers to create an illusion of depth.

Dewing began as a lithographic apprentice in Boston. From 1876 he studied at the Académie Julian in Paris with Gustave Boulanger and Jules Lefebvre, where he learned an academic technique. In 1880 he moved to New York and married Maria Oakey Dewing, an accomplished painter. Their son died in infancy. The Dewings spent summers at the Cornish Art Colony in New Hampshire for two decades. He was noted for figure paintings of aristocratic women and taught at the Art Students League of New York.

Le Prince first studied painting in his native Metz. Around 1750 he travelled to Paris, sponsored by Charles Louis Auguste Fouquet de Belle-Isle, and became a leading student of François Boucher. His early paintings compare with the rococo of his master. In 1758 he journeyed to Russia to work for Catherine the Great at the Imperial Palace in St. Petersburg, and he stayed five years. On his return he turned the drawings he brought back into paintings and etchings, and in 1765 he became a full member of the Académie.

Friant came from the commune of Dieuze, where his father worked as a locksmith and his mother as a dressmaker. Madame Parisot, the wife of a local chemist, often hired his mother, and the childless Parisots took an early interest in the boy. In 1871 Madame Parisot fled with him to Nancy after the annexation of Alsatia. He exhibited at the Paris Salon throughout his life. He worked in charcoal and oil, and he also used photographs to prepare finished paintings. Later he served as a professor of painting at the École des Beaux-Arts.

Matsys came from Leuven, and according to tradition he trained as an ironsmith before he became a painter. Early accounts of his life are composed largely of legend. One of four children, he was born to Joost Matsys and Catherine van Kincken between April and September 1466. Legend says he abandoned the forge to win his wife, who thought painting a more romantic profession. He was active in Antwerp for over 20 years. His many works have religious roots and satirical tendencies, and he is regarded as the founder of the Antwerp school of painting.

Van Loo belonged to a dynasty of painters of Dutch origin and was the son of Louis-Abraham van Loo. He followed his brother Jean-Baptiste to Turin and then to Rome in 1712, where he studied under Benedetto Luti and the sculptor Pierre Le Gros. After leaving Italy in 1723 he worked in Paris and studied at the Académie royale. He won the Prix de Rome in 1724. Later King Victor Amadeus II of Sardinia employed him to paint a series of subjects from Tasso. His work covers religion, history, mythology, portraiture, allegory and genre scenes.

Van Schuppen studied painting in Antwerp and became a master in the local guild of St Luke. He then left the city and settled in Paris in 1655. There he became a pupil of Robert Nanteuil, the foremost French engraver of his time. The Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture admitted him in 1663. He left about 119 prints, mainly portraits of famous people of his day such as Cardinal Mazarin and King Louis XIV, and most were made after paintings by other artists. His son Jacob became a prominent painter in Vienna.

Geyser, whose father and elder brother were Lutheran theologians, began law studies at the University of Leipzig but also took art lessons from Adam Friedrich Oeser. When Oeser became first director of the new Academy of Fine Arts in 1764, he hired Geyser as an assistant engraving teacher. After 1770 Geyser worked as an independent book illustrator. He married Oeser's daughter Wilhelmine. His illustrations, some for first editions of works by Goethe and Wieland, earned him a country estate in Eutritzsch. His son Gottlieb Wilhelm also became a graphic artist.

Van Brussel, a native of Haarlem, was a pupil of Johan Bernhard Brandhof, Christiaan Henning and Wybrand Hendriks, according to the RKD. He later taught Woutherus Mol. Among his best etchings is a set of twenty-one landscapes with figures. He was known for his set designs for the Amsterdam Theatre and Het Loo Palace, and in Haarlem he made many for the amateur playhouse society Kunstliefde. Like many Dutch painters of his time, he paid great attention to the skies in his works, because the land was often relatively featureless.

Carpeaux, the son of a mason from Valenciennes, studied first under François Rude. He entered the École des Beaux-Arts and won the Prix de Rome in 1854. In Rome he studied the works of Michelangelo, Donatello and Verrocchio. There he acquired a taste for movement and spontaneity, which he joined with the great principles of baroque art. He sought real life subjects in the streets and broke with the classical tradition. He was an admirer of Napoléon III and followed the emperor through the north of France until he arranged a meeting at Amiens.

Diemer, who studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich with Gabriel Hackl and Alexander von Liezen-Mayer, first won fame with panoramic paintings of battles. In 1894 he spent six months in Innsbruck creating a panorama of 1000 square meters that depicts the Battles of Bergisel. It is one of only thirty surviving panoramas from that period. Another panorama showed the Battle of Bazeilles and is now lost. For the Deutsches Museum in Munich he created several works, among them a Roman aqueduct for the hydraulic engineering display. He is now known primarily for marine paintings and postcard designs.

Gros began learning to draw at six from his father, a miniature painter, and his mother was also a painter. Towards the close of 1785 he chose to enter the studio of Jacques-Louis David, while following classes at the Collège Mazarin. During the Revolution he was forced to leave France and moved to Genoa. His portrait of Napoleon Bonaparte at the Battle of Arcole brought him to public attention and gained the patronage of Napoleon. After traveling with the army for several years he returned to Paris. He produced large battle paintings and was a successful portraitist.

Davis studied at the American Academy of Fine Arts and the New-York Drawing Association, then dropped out of school to become a lithographer. From 1826 he worked as a draftsman for the architect Josiah Brady, an early exponent of the Gothic Revival. His first independent career was as an architectural illustrator. Friends, especially the painter John Trumbull, convinced him to design buildings. He then joined the office of Ithiel Town, a firm of the Greek Revival, where he had access to the best architectural library in the country.

Allegrini, son of the painter Flaminio Allegrini da Cantiano, studied with Giuseppe Cesari and was drawn early to the art of Pietro da Cortona, though the full Baroque stayed alien to him. Early sources place him in Savona Cathedral and in palaces in Genoa. It remains unclear whether those commissions belong to him or to his father. He worked mostly in Rome, where many of his canvases and frescoes survive in churches and palaces. Around 1650 he painted an altarpiece of Saint Catherine for the church of Santi Domenico e Sisto.

Currier attended public school until fifteen, when he was apprenticed to the Boston printing firm of William and John Pendleton, the first successful lithographers in the United States. He learned the process in their shop. After working for a Philadelphia lithographer, he moved to New York City and started a short-lived firm, then began his own lithographic business. At first it printed sheet music, letterheads and handbills. Soon he took his work in a new direction, creating pictures of current events. He headed the company Currier and Ives.

Matham, son of the engraver Jacob Matham, was born in Haarlem and was the brother of the engravers Jan and Theodor. He joined the Haarlem civic guard and was painted by Frans Hals as its flag-bearer in 1627. He made drawings after Hals' paintings, most notably a sketch of a portrait of Isaac Massa. In 1640 he took part in a Dutch embassy to the king of Morocco, led by Antonius de Liedekerke, and made some engravings there. He married three times. In the 1650s he lived in The Hague, where he died.

Stachiewicz studied at the Kraków Academy of Fine Arts with Władysław Łuszczkiewicz and Florian Cynk, then at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich with Otto Seitz. After graduating he took an extensive trip to Italy and Greece, ending in Jerusalem. He settled in Kraków, where he painted portraits, historical scenes and religious art. He designed mosaics for the Basilica of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. He refused an offer to direct the Kraków Academy, because the post would have required him to fire some of his old instructors. He also illustrated works by Adam Mickiewicz.

The son of a Leiden goldsmith and diamond setter, Van Mieris preferred drawing to his father's trade and studied with Abraham Toorenvliet, a glazier who kept a school of design. He soon left for the workshops of Gerard Dou and Abraham van den Tempel. From them he acquired the Leiden fijnschilder manner rather than the Amsterdam finish of Rembrandt's disciples. He seldom chose panels larger than 12 to 15 inches. He was the leading member of a Leiden family of painters. His sons Jan and Willem also painted.

Vigneron came to Paris to study painting and worked in the workshop of Gustave Gautherot before joining the school of Antoine-Jean Gros. He also attended the Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture in Toulouse, focusing on miniatures and sculpture. His talent earned him an academy prize for a bas-relief composition depicting Aristides. Back in Paris in 1812 he devoted himself to portraiture and exhibited for the first time at the Salon. His paintings, drawings and lithographs hung in the Salon until 1865. He was an early practitioner of lithography during its formative years in France.

Thaulow, the son of a wealthy chemist from Christiania, was educated at the Academy of Art in Copenhagen. He then studied with Hans Gude at the Baden School of Art in Karlsruhe. In 1879 he arrived in Skagen with his friend Christian Krohg, who persuaded him to spend the summer and autumn there. They crossed from Norway in Thaulow's little boat. He had specialized in marine painting but turned to Skagen's favorite subjects, the fishermen and the boats on the shore. After that stay he returned to Norway and became one of the leading young figures in its art scene.

Born and dead in Delft, Van Mierevelt was the son of a goldsmith, who apprenticed him to the copperplate engraver Hieronymus Wierix. He later became a pupil of Willem Willemz and Augusteyn of Delft. Anthonie van Montfoort had admired two of his early engravings, Christ and the Samaritan and Judith and Holofernes, and invited him to enter his school at Utrecht. Devoting himself first to still lifes, he eventually took up portraiture. So many commissions came in that he employed numerous assistants, and hundreds of portraits were turned out in factory fashion. Over 500 paintings have been attributed to him.

Munsterhjelm, born at Toivoniemi Manor in Tuulos, was first sent by his father to the Turku Maritime School. In the early 1860s he studied art at Düsseldorf with Werner Holmberg and Oswald Achenbach, and at Karlsruhe under Hans Gude. His landscapes were influenced by the romanticism of the Düsseldorf school and often presented nature as a mood rather than a realistic subject. Alexander III bought his October Evening After the First Snowfall, which is now in the Ateneum in Helsinki. Two other works were shown at the Paris Exposition of 1878. He married Olga Tanninen, and they had four children.

Van Mieris studied under his father, Frans van Mieris the Elder, a successful genre painter in Leiden. At 19 he took over the family workshop after his father died. He had barely finished his training. It would take another two years before he entered the Leiden painters' guild, and he set out to uphold his father's reputation as a Leiden fijnschilder, a painter in the fine manner. His work consists mostly of genre and portraiture, with some landscapes and a few sculptures. Later his genre works depicted scenes from upper-class society.

Rejected three times by the École des Beaux Arts, Rodin trained at an applied arts school in Paris and in various studios and workshops. He gained public attention and individual commissions only in his late 30s. His first major figure was inspired by a trip to Italy in 1875. He became known for the boldly expressive physicality of works such as The Kiss, The Burghers of Calais and The Gates of Hell. Critics called many of his sculptures unfinished or fragmented, because they departed from traditional themes of mythology and allegory. He refused to change his style.

Born Georges Joseph van Sluijters in Paris, De Feure moved to The Hague at two and grew up there as the son of a Dutch architect and a Belgian mother. He was one of eleven students admitted to the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam, but he left quickly for Paris because he felt formal academic training had nothing to offer him. He never again took up formal studies. Jules Chéret influenced his posters for the café concert. He became the key designer of Siegfried Bing for L'Art Nouveau.
